record.original_question: An odd prime p is regular when p does not divide the numerator of the Bernoulli number B_k for every k = 2, 4, ..., p-3. Are there infinitely many regular primes?

evidence.quote: If an odd prime number p does not divide the numerator of the Bernoulli number B_k for every k=2,4,...,p-3, then p is called a regular prime. The question whether there are infinitely many regular primes remains open.

artifact.self_contained_problem: Let the Bernoulli numbers $B_n$ be defined by the generating function $\frac{x}{e^x - 1} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} B_n \frac{x^n}{n!}$, so that $B_0 = 1$, $B_1 = -1/2$, $B_2 = 1/6$, $B_4 = -1/30$, etc. An odd prime $p$ is called regular if $p$ does not divide the numerator (when written in lowest terms) of $B_k$ for any even integer $k$ with $2 \le k \le p-3$. Otherwise $p$ is called irregular.\n\nProve or disprove: there exist infinitely many regular primes.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a classical long-standing open problem in number theory. It is conjectured (with heuristic evidence due to Siegel suggesting density $e^{-1/2} \approx 60.65\%$) that infinitely many regular primes exist, but no proof is known. In contrast, it has been proved (by Jensen, 1915) that there are infinitely many irregular primes.

status_evidence.title: Regular prime - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: It is conjectured that there are infinitely many regular primes. More precisely Siegel (1964) conjectured that e^{-1/2}, or about 60.65%, of all primes are regular. Neither conjecture has been proven to date.
status_evidence.claim: The infinitude of regular primes is an open conjecture.
